stories.title: Iran Warns It Could Strike Oil Fields — Petrol Prices at Risk
stories.headline_kid: A country called Iran says it will hit back at oil and gas fields if the US attacks it — and that could make petrol cost more, even in Singapore.
summary: Iran is a country in the Middle East that has been in a tense stand-off with the United States. This weekend, a group linked to Iran's top security body warned that if American forces attack Iran's oil and gas sites, Iran will strike back by hitting oil fields in Saudi Arabia and the UAE, plus gas fields in Qatar and Israel.

This matters because the Middle East is where a huge part of the world's oil and gas comes from — the fuel that powers cars, buses, and even the gas stoves some families use for cooking. When fighting threatens oil-producing areas, less fuel can reach the market.

Think of it like a popular snack running low in the shops — when something is scarce, sellers often raise the price. If oil supply drops because of fighting, petrol pump prices around the world, including in Singapore, could climb.

For now, this is a warning and not an actual attack. But because Singapore has no oil of its own and buys almost all its fuel from overseas, families here would feel it directly at the pump if tensions boil over.

lenses.me: If petrol gets pricier, your family's Grab or taxi rides might cost a bit more too.
lenses.family: Parents may notice higher prices when pumping petrol for the family car or when paying for cooking gas at home.
lenses.friends: Your friends whose parents drive to school might hear grown-ups talking about rising fuel costs at the dinner table.
lenses.nation: Singapore imports almost all its energy, so trouble in the Middle East can quickly affect prices here.
lenses.world: Countries everywhere are watching closely, since a bigger conflict could disrupt oil supplies for the whole world.

stories.title: Missing Singaporean Woman Found Safe in Cambodia
stories.headline_kid: A Singaporean woman who went missing has been found in Cambodia, and she says she left on her own to work as an English teacher.
summary: A Singaporean woman named Aishah Siregar had gone missing, worrying her family here at home. She has now been found by police in Cambodia, and she recorded a video explaining what happened.

In the video, Aishah said she chose to travel to Cambodia by herself to work as an English teacher. She also said she was not forced into scam activities — a serious problem where some people are tricked or trapped into working for online scam gangs in parts of Southeast Asia.

This case reminds us why it's so important to tell trusted adults where you are going, especially when travelling far from home. It also shows how online scam centres have become a real danger in the region, with some victims being deceived by fake job offers.
Aishah's family and the Singapore authorities had been searching for her, and her being found safe is a relief. Investigations may continue to make sure everything she shared checks out.

lenses.me: It's a good reminder to always let your parents know where you are, even during school holidays or trips.
lenses.family: Families can talk about staying safe when travelling and the importance of checking in regularly.
lenses.friends: Classmates might discuss why some people fall for scam job offers, especially online.
lenses.nation: Singapore works closely with other countries to help find and protect its citizens abroad.
lenses.world: Scam centres trapping workers have become a serious cross-border problem across Southeast Asia.

stories.title: China Sends Ships and Planes Near Contested Sea Area
stories.headline_kid: China held military drills near a disputed sandbank in the South China Sea — a busy sea route that ships from Singapore use every day.
summary: China's navy and coast guard carried out joint air and sea drills around Scarborough Shoal, a shallow, rocky area in the South China Sea. China calls it Huangyan Dao, but other countries, like the Philippines, also claim it as their own.

The South China Sea is one of the busiest sea routes in the world. Huge cargo ships carrying everything from electronics to food pass through it — including many ships heading to and from Singapore's port, one of the busiest in the world.

China said the drills were a response to actions by other countries that it felt were 'undermining' peace in the region. But when big countries show off their military strength in shared waters, it can make shipping companies nervous and raise concerns about safety at sea.
Singapore does not claim any part of the South China Sea, but as a small country that depends heavily on trade, it wants the waters to stay calm and open for all ships to pass through safely.

lenses.me: Many everyday items you use, like toys or gadgets, might travel through this sea route on their way to Singapore.
lenses.family: If shipping gets disrupted, some imported goods your family buys could take longer to arrive or cost more.
lenses.friends: Your friends who like ships or geography might find it interesting how one shoal can cause such big disagreements.
lenses.nation: Singapore relies on open, safe sea lanes for trade, so it closely watches tensions in the South China Sea.
lenses.world: Several countries claim parts of this sea, and disagreements here can affect global trade and peace in Asia.

stories.title: Big Election Result Next Door in Malaysia
stories.headline_kid: Malaysia's Negeri Sembilan state just voted, and the ruling coalition led by PM Anwar Ibrahim's party suffered a big loss.
summary: Negeri Sembilan, a state in Malaysia, held elections this past weekend. The results are in: an alliance called BN-PN won a huge majority of 25 seats, while Pakatan Harapan (PH), the coalition supporting Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim, lost badly.

Some very senior PH leaders lost their own seats, including Malaysia's Transport Minister Anthony Loke and the state's caretaker chief minister. This is the second setback in a row for PH, after a similarly rough result in Johor's election last month.

Why does this matter to us in Singapore? Malaysia is our closest neighbour, connected by the Causeway and the Second Link. Political changes there can affect things families here care about, like the supply of fresh vegetables and eggs, and how smoothly traffic flows across the border.
It's a reminder that elections, even in a neighbouring state, can shift the mood of a whole country and shape decisions that ripple across the Causeway to Singapore.

lenses.me: If you've travelled to Johor Bahru with family for weekend trips, changes in Malaysia's politics could affect things like border checks.
lenses.family: Many households buy Malaysian-grown vegetables and eggs, so political changes there can sometimes affect food prices.
lenses.friends: Classmates whose families have relatives in Malaysia might hear more discussion about this at home.
lenses.nation: Singapore watches Malaysia's elections closely because of our deep trade and travel links.
lenses.world: This result shows how public opinion in Southeast Asia can shift quickly, affecting regional politics.

stories.title: Singaporean Turns Homesickness Into a Spice Business in London
stories.headline_kid: A Singaporean woman who once couldn't cook now runs a spice business bringing rempah and sambal flavours to homes across Britain.
summary: Shu Han Lee left Singapore at 18 to study in London. Back then, she didn't even know how to cook — but her mother insisted she pack a small amount of rempah, a fragrant spice paste used in many Singaporean and Malaysian dishes.
Far from home and missing familiar flavours, Shu Han taught herself to cook using that rempah as her starting point. What began as simple homesickness slowly grew into something much bigger.

Today, she runs Rempapa Spice Co, a company that helps British home cooks make dishes with rempah, sambal, and other flavours many Singaporean families grew up eating. She has also written two cookbooks to share these recipes with people who may never have tried them before.

Her journey shows how food can carry a piece of home wherever you go, and how something as simple as a spice paste can become a bridge between cultures, introducing Singaporean flavours to kitchens thousands of kilometres away.

lenses.me: You might already enjoy dishes made with rempah at home, like curry or sambal, without realising how special they are.
lenses.family: Your family's home-cooked meals could inspire someone far away, just like Shu Han's mother inspired her.
lenses.friends: Friends who love cooking might be curious about starting their own food projects one day.
lenses.nation: Stories like this help spread Singapore's food culture to people around the world.
lenses.world: It shows how migration and food can connect different cultures across countries.
